methods.label: Expose a cube inside the logarithm
methods.explanation:
Since \(f\) uses the ratio \((1+x)/(1-x)\), compute that same ratio for the new argument. Let
\[
u=\frac{3x+x^3}{1+3x^2}.
\]
The denominator \(1+3x^2\) is positive. Combining terms reveals two cubes:
\[
1+u=\frac{1+3x+3x^2+x^3}{1+3x^2}
=\frac{(1+x)^3}{1+3x^2},
\]
\[
1-u=\frac{1-3x+3x^2-x^3}{1+3x^2}
=\frac{(1-x)^3}{1+3x^2}.
\]
Because \(-1<x<1\), both \(1+x\) and \(1-x\) are positive. Consequently \(1+u>0\) and \(1-u>0\), which proves \(-1<u<1\); the requested function value is defined.

Dividing the two expressions cancels their common positive denominator. The logarithm power rule then gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
f(u)
&=\log\left(\frac{(1+x)^3}{(1-x)^3}\right)\\
&=3\log\left(\frac{1+x}{1-x}\right)\\
&=\boxed{3f(x)}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The logarithm arguments are positive throughout the given interval, so every step is valid. The answer is choice \(\text{C}\).
